name: Ful, Sokoto dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: Betonung. 11. Im Ful herrscht der Starkton. Er liegt stets auf der vorletzten Silbe des Wortes. Die Silbe mit dem Starkton, sowie auch die vorangehenden Silben desselben Wortes haben außerdem Hochton, dagegen die letzte Silbe, also die auf den Starkton folgende, wird tieftonig gesprochen. Die Regel ist also einfach diese: Alle Silben mit Ausnahme der letzten haben Hochton, die vorletzte hat neben dem Hochton noch den Starkton, die letzte Silbe ist tieftonig. Die meisten Wörter, die von dieser Regel abweichen, weisen sich schon dadurch als Fremdwörter aus. Es gibt allerdings einige einsilbige Wörter, die keinen eigenen Ton haben, sondern enklitisch behandelt werden, d. h. sie lehnen sich an das vorangehende Wort und werden mit diesem zu einer Einheit zusammengezogen, z. B. o námi er aß (der Starkton ruht auf nā), dagegen o nāmi di er aß sie (die Fische); das di lehnt sich an nāmi, bildet mit ihm gleichsam ein Wort; deshalb rückt der Starkton vor und ruht nun auf mi, so liegt er also wieder auf der zweitletzten Silbe dieser Worteinheit. Häufig, aber nicht immer, erhält dann die Silbe mit dem Starkton, auch wenn sie sonst kurz ist, langen Vokal ... Weil der Starkton nach den eben angegebenen Regeln stets ohne Schwierigkeiten festzustellen ist, ist eine besondere Bezeichnung desselben nicht nötig. Nur wo sich Abweichungen von der Regel finden, ist die Lage des Starktones durch ein über dem Vokal angedeutet.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: The one title-keyword hit for west2454 (Yenkimaleki & van Heuven 2019, Dutch Journal of Applied Linguistics) is a Glottolog misattribution: its Crossref abstract and landing page concern English L2 prosody training for Farsi-speaking interpreter trainees and never mention Fulfulde, Fula or Niger (priority none). The language is not in the catalog. The best first-hand stress statement actually read is Westermann 1909 pp. 197-198 (Sokoto Ful, a Glottolog dialect of west2454; HathiTrust full view, held by the project): fixed penultimate 'Starkton' over word+enclitic, non-final syllables high-pitched, final low, loanwords the only exceptions. Supporting fragments: Klingenheben 1927 pp. 22, 58 (penultimate accent, pan-Fula, snippets) and Sow 2003 p. 49 ('syllabe accentuée' with vowel lengthening in Gaawoore, no placement rule visible in preview). Peace Corps 1993 (full PDF held by the project) is silent. Not obtained: Alkali 2019 HKU thesis on Sokoto Fula phonology (not reachable by automated download direct, via direct download and r.jina.ai; abstract silent on stress; priority high as the only modern phonology of a west2454 variety) and Bidaud & Prost 1982 Liptako manual (HathiTrust search-only, Harvard print; priority medium).

new_statements.translation: Stress. 11. In Ful a stress accent (Starkton) prevails. It always lies on the penultimate syllable of the word. The stressed syllable, as well as the syllables of the same word that precede it, additionally have high pitch, whereas the last syllable, i.e. the one following the stress, is pronounced low. The rule is thus simply this: all syllables except the last have high pitch, the penult has the stress in addition to the high pitch, the last syllable is low. Most words that deviate from this rule thereby reveal themselves as loanwords. There are, however, some monosyllabic words that have no accent of their own but are treated as enclitics [...]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (Starkton) falls on the penultimate syllable of every native word; pre-stress syllables and the stressed syllable are high-pitched, the final syllable low. Monosyllabic enclitics (object pronouns, am 'my', ma 'your', negative ta, passive ma) form one accentual word with their host, so stress shifts rightward onto the new penult (o námi 'he ate' vs o nāmí ɗi 'he ate them'), the newly stressed vowel often lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Westermann says all pre-tonic syllables carry high pitch but no secondary stress, and reports no separate sentence stress ('ein eigentlicher Satzton neben dem Starkton nicht vorhanden'): each word's Starkton is realized with equal force.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords deviate (marked with a diacritic where they do); enclitics shift stress to the host+clitic penult (§11, §36, §57 'mi lilá ta', §69 passive -ma with lengthened stressed vowel 'lilīma'); future -ai unstressed with 'Ton' on the first syllable (mi yíai) versus negative preterite with long stressed -ā- (mi yi'āi) (§51, §58); yes/no questions may slightly raise the pitch of the final syllable (§12).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word plus following enclitics (an accentual 'Worteinheit'); statement is impressionistic (1909), based mainly on one Sokoto-born informant (Audu Hamadu) interviewed in Lomé, Togo, partly through Hausa; Klingenheben 1927 criticizes the Handbuch's reliability. Modern descriptions of other Fula varieties (Arnott 1970 Gombe, McIntosh 1984 Kaceccereere, Breedveld 1995 Maasina, Stennes 1967 Adamawa) describe initial/weight-sensitive or morphological stress, not a fixed penult, so this compilation should carry a caution flag until Alkali 2019 or Bidaud & Prost 1982 is read.
new_statements.identity_note: Westermann 1909 describes 'der in und um Sokoto.. gesprochene Dialekt des Ful' (informant Audu Hamadu of Sokoto, recorded in Lomé, Togo, 1907), i.e. Sokoto Fulfulde of NW Nigeria. Ethnologue/Glottolog place Sokoto State Fula under fuh/west2454 (Glottolog files both Westermann 1909 and Alkali 2019 'Sokoto Fula' here), but it is the eastern edge of the fuh area, not the Liptaako (Dori, Burkina) / Téra-Gaawoore (W Niger) core that Bidaud & Prost 1982 and Sow 2003 describe. Sow 2003 (Gaawoore, Lacroix's parler no. 15 'Gaoɓe') appears silent on stress placement. The 1909 penult claim conflicts with modern accounts of neighbouring Fula varieties (initial/weight-sensitive in Arnott 1970 Gombe [fuv], Breedveld 1995 Maasina [ffm]; morphological in Stennes 1967 Adamawa [fub], already in the catalog), so flag with caution.

new_statements.translation: In Ful the strong stress predominates. It always falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. The syllable with the strong stress, and also the preceding syllables of the same word, have high pitch besides, whereas the last syllable, i.e. the one following the strong stress, is spoken with low pitch. The rule is thus simply this: all syllables except the last have high pitch, the penultimate has the strong stress in addition to the high pitch, the last syllable is low-pitched. Most words that deviate from this rule thereby show themselves to be loanwords. ... o námi 'he ate' (the stress rests on nā), but o nāmí di 'he ate them (the fish)' ... hence the stress moves forward and now rests on mi.
new_statements.citation: Westermann, Diedrich (1909). Handbuch der Ful-Sprache: Wörterbuch, Grammatik, Übungen und Texte. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer (Ernst Vohsen). Lautlehre §11 'Betonung', pp. 197-198. Data: Ful of Sokoto (informant Audu Hamadu of Sokoto, recorded Lomé 1907, Vorwort p. iii); Glottolog places Sokoto [soko1247] as a dialect of west2454.
new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word stress, computed over the phonological word including enclitics (stress shifts rightward when an enclitic pronoun attaches), with a superimposed pitch contour (all non-final syllables high, final low), stressed syllable often lengthened, exceptions confined to loanwords; explicitly no separate sentence stress observed. This is a 1909 statement for the Sokoto variety, which Glottolog files under west2454 but which lies at the eastern (Nigerian) edge of the language; nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title states the rule for the western-Niger/Liptako varieties proper, although Sow 2003 p. 49 confirms an accented syllable with vowel lengthening in Gaawoore and Klingenheben 1927 (pp. 22, 58) presupposes a penultimate accent for Ful generally.

sources.note: Lautlehre §11 'Betonung' (pp.197-198): Ful has a stress accent (Starkton) that always lies on the penultimate syllable of the word; all syllables but the last are high-pitched, the penult carries stress+high pitch, the final is low; deviating words are mostly loans; monosyllabic enclitics (object pronouns, am 'my', ma 'your', negative ta, passive ma) join the preceding word so stress moves to the new penult, often with vowel lengthening; no separate sentence stress observed; §12 yes/no questions slightly raise the final syllable. Vorwort p.iii: material is 'der in und um Sokoto.. gesprochene…
